cards.title: What is a **class**, and what is an **object** (also called an **instance**) made from it?
cards.body:
A class is a blueprint that describes a kind of thing; an object (instance) is one actual thing built from that blueprint.

Think of a house plan and the houses built from it. You write the plan once, and you can build as many houses as you like. Each house is separate: painting one red does not repaint the others.

Example: `class Dog:` describes dogs in general. `rex = Dog()` and `fido = Dog()` each create one **object**; both are instances of the class `Dog`, but they are two separate things.

Key idea: Types you already know are classes too. `3` is an instance of `int`, and `[1, 2]` is an instance of `list`.

Watch out: The class is not one of its own instances. `Dog` is the blueprint; `rex` is a dog.
cards.searchQuery: python class vs object instance blueprint

cards.title:
What does this print?

```python
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

pet = Dog("Rex")
print(pet.name)
```
cards.body:
`Rex`

`Dog("Rex")` builds a new object and then automatically runs its **`__init__`** method, the setup method of a class. The new object arrives as `self`, and `"Rex"` arrives as `name`.

The line `self.name = name` stores the value inside the object. A value stored inside an object is called an **attribute**, and you read it with a dot: `pet.name`.

Key idea: `__init__` runs once, at the moment an instance is created. Use it to give the object its starting attributes.

Watch out: The name has two underscores on each side. `_init_` or `init` is just an ordinary method that Python never calls for you.
cards.searchQuery: python __init__ constructor attribute self name

cards.title: What is the difference between an **attribute** and a **method** of an object?
cards.body:
An attribute is a piece of data stored in an object (`pet.name`); a method is a function defined in the class that works on the object (`pet.speak()`).

Both are reached with a dot. The telltale sign is the parentheses: a method is called with `()`, an attribute is only read.

Example: For a `Dog` object, `pet.name` gives the stored name `"Rex"`, while `pet.speak()` runs the code of the `speak` method, which might return `"Woof"`.

Tip: A method is written inside the class with `def`, exactly like a function, and its first parameter is `self`.

Watch out: Leaving out the parentheses, as in `pet.speak`, does not run the method. It just gives you the method itself.
cards.searchQuery: python attribute vs method class dot notation

cards.title: Inside a method, what is **`self`**?
cards.body:
`self` is the object the method was called on: Python passes it in automatically as the first argument.

When you write `a.add()`, Python treats it like `Counter.add(a)`. That is why every method lists `self` first, yet you never type it when you call the method. It is how the method knows which object's data to use.

Why: A class can have many instances. `self` lets one method definition work on whichever instance called it.

Watch out: To store data on the object you must write `self.count = 0`. A bare `count = 0` inside `__init__` makes an ordinary local variable that disappears when the method ends.

Tip: `self` is only a convention, not a keyword, but everyone uses it. Stick with it.
cards.searchQuery: python self parameter explained method first argument

cards.title:
What does this print?

```python
class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.count = 0

    def add(self):
        self.count += 1

a = Counter()
b = Counter()
a.add()
a.add()
b.add()
print(a.count, b.count)
```
cards.body:
`2 1`

Each instance has its own `count`, created by `__init__` on its own `self`. Calling `a.add()` twice raises `a.count` to 2. Calling `b.add()` once raises `b.count` to 1.

Key idea: Attributes set through `self` belong to one object. Changing one instance does not touch another.

Example: Think of two separate click counters, one in each hand. Pressing the left one never changes the right one.

Watch out: Both objects start at 0 because each ran `__init__`. Nothing links `a.count` and `b.count`.
cards.searchQuery: python class counter method self.count instances

cards.title:
A vector here is just a pair of numbers, like an arrow. What does this print?

```python
class Vector:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __str__(self):
        return f"({self.x}, {self.y})"

v = Vector(3, 4)
print(v)
```
cards.body:
`(3, 4)`

`print` turns an object into text by calling its **`__str__`** method, which Python runs for you. Here it returns the f-string `"(3, 4)"`, and that is what appears.

Without `__str__`, `print(v)` shows something like `<__main__.Vector object at 0x7f...>`: the class name and a memory address, which is useless for reading.

Watch out: `__str__` must return a string, not print one. If it used `print` inside and returned nothing, Python would raise a `TypeError`.

Tip: Methods whose names start and end with two underscores are called special methods. You rarely call them yourself; Python calls them at the right moment.
cards.searchQuery: python __str__ method print object readable text

cards.body:
`11 22`

When Python sees `a + b` it calls `a.__add__(b)`. The left operand is `self` and the right one is `other`. The method adds the matching parts, `1 + 10` and `2 + 20`, and returns a brand-new `Vector`.

Key idea: The method returns a new object. Neither of the two original vectors is changed.

Watch out: Without `__add__`, the same line fails with `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +`. Python has no idea how to add two arbitrary objects until you teach it.

Tip: Other operators work the same way: `__sub__` for `-`, `__mul__` for `*`, `__eq__` for `==`.
cards.searchQuery: python operator overloading __add__ vector class

cards.title: What is **inheritance** in a Python class?
cards.body:
Inheritance builds a new class (the subclass) on top of an existing one (the parent class), so the subclass automatically gets the parent's attributes and methods.

You write the parent in brackets after the new class name: `class Thermometer(Sensor):`. Anything `Sensor` can do, a `Thermometer` can do too, and the subclass can add new methods or replace (override) an inherited one by defining a method with the same name.

Why: Related classes usually share behavior. Inheritance lets you write that shared code once instead of copying it.

Watch out: Use it for an "is a" relationship: a thermometer is a sensor. If the relationship is only "has a", store the other object as an attribute instead.
cards.searchQuery: python inheritance subclass parent class definition

cards.body:
`sensor T1`

`Thermometer` has an empty body (`pass` means "do nothing"), yet it works. When Python cannot find `__init__` or `describe` in `Thermometer`, it looks in the parent class `Sensor` and uses those. So `Thermometer("T1")` runs `Sensor.__init__`, and `t.describe()` runs `Sensor.describe`.

Key idea: A subclass is searched first, then its parent.

Watch out: If the subclass defines its own `__init__`, the parent's no longer runs automatically. Call `super().__init__(name)` inside it to run the parent's setup too.
cards.searchQuery: python inheritance subclass uses parent init and method

cards.title: What is a NumPy **ndarray**?
cards.body:
An ndarray is NumPy's grid of numbers: every element has the same type, and all of them sit together in one block of memory.

**NumPy** is a library, a collection of ready-made code you bring in with `import numpy as np`. Its main object is the **ndarray**, short for "n-dimensional array". You make one from a list with `np.array([1, 2, 3])`, or fill one with zeros or ones using `np.zeros(3)` and `np.ones((2, 2))`.

Why: A Python list can hold a mix of things, each stored separately. An ndarray holds one kind of number, packed tightly, and that is exactly what makes it fast.

Watch out: An ndarray's size is fixed when it is created. Unlike a list, it has no `append` that grows it in place.
cards.searchQuery: numpy ndarray definition n-dimensional array same type
refs: NumPy User Guide: the absolute basics for beginners

cards.title:
What does this print?

```python
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(2, 10, 3))
```
cards.body:
`[2 5 8]`

`np.arange(start, stop, step)` counts from `start` in jumps of `step` and stops before `stop`. Here it gives 2, then 5, then 8. The next value, 11, is past 10, so it is left out.

Key idea: The `stop` value is never included. This matches `range()` from Python, except that `np.arange` returns an array.

Watch out: With a fractional step such as 0.1, rounding error can make the number of elements surprising. For evenly spaced points, `np.linspace` is safer.
cards.searchQuery: numpy arange start stop step excludes stop
refs: NumPy User Guide: the absolute basics for beginners

cards.title:
What does this print?

```python
import numpy as np
print(np.linspace(0, 1, 5))
```
cards.body:
`[0.   0.25 0.5  0.75 1.  ]`

`np.linspace(start, stop, num)` gives exactly `num` evenly spaced values, and it includes both ends. With 5 points between 0 and 1 there are 4 gaps, so each step is $1/4 = 0.25$.

Key idea: You choose how many points you want, and NumPy works out the step. With `np.arange` it is the other way round.

Tip: `linspace` is the usual way to build a time axis, for example 1000 sample times between 0 s and 1 s.

Watch out: The values are floats, so they print with decimal points, padded to line up in columns.

cards.title: What is an array's **shape**, and how do **ndim** and **axis** relate to it?
cards.body:
The shape is a tuple of the array's length along each axis, such as `(2, 3)` for 2 rows and 3 columns; `ndim` is how many numbers the shape has.

An **axis** is one direction of the array. Axis 0 runs down the rows, axis 1 runs across the columns. A table with 2 rows and 3 columns has shape `(2, 3)`, so `ndim` is 2 and its `size` (total number of elements) is $2 \times 3 = 6$.

Example: A list of three readings becomes a 1-D array with shape `(3,)`. The comma is needed: Python writes a one-item tuple that way.

Watch out: This is a new use of the word axis. Before it meant a side of a graph; here it means a direction along the data.
cards.searchQuery: numpy array shape ndim axis tuple rows columns
refs: NumPy User Guide: the absolute basics for beginners

cards.title:
What does this print?

```python
import numpy as np
z = np.zeros((2, 3))
print(z.shape, z.ndim, z.size)
```
cards.body:
`(2, 3) 2 6`

`np.zeros` takes the shape as one tuple, so there are two sets of parentheses: the outer ones belong to the function and the inner ones make the tuple. The result is a 2-row, 3-column array of `0.0`, so `shape` is `(2, 3)`, `ndim` is 2 and `size` is 6.

Watch out: `np.zeros(2, 3)` is an error. The second argument is read as the data type, and 3 is not one.

Tip: `np.ones((2, 3))` works the same way and fills with `1.0` instead.
cards.searchQuery: numpy zeros shape tuple ndim size

cards.title:
What does this print?

```python
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3],
              [4, 5, 6]])
print(a[:, 1:])
```
cards.body:
A 2×2 array with rows `[2 3]` and `[5 6]`.

**Slicing** an array uses `start:stop` for each axis, with the axes separated by commas. The first part, `:`, picks every row. The second part, `1:`, picks columns from position 1 to the end, so columns 1 and 2 (the values 2, 3 and 5, 6).

Key idea: Each axis gets its own slice, in axis order: rows first, then columns. As with lists, `stop` is excluded and counting starts at 0.

Example: `a[1, :]` picks row 1 only, giving `[4 5 6]`. `a[:, 0]` picks column 0, giving `[1 4]`.

cards.title: What is a **Boolean mask**, and what does indexing an array with one do?
cards.body:
A Boolean mask is an array of True/False values with the same shape as the data; indexing with it keeps only the elements where the mask is True.

Comparing an array with a number builds a mask: for `x = np.array([4, 9, 2, 7])`, the expression `x > 5` is `[False True False True]`. Then `x[x > 5]` is `[9 7]`.

Example: To keep only the sensor readings above 3.3, write `readings[readings > 3.3]`.

Watch out: To combine conditions use `&` and `|` with each condition in parentheses: `x[(x > 2) & (x < 8)]` gives `[4 7]`. The words `and` and `or` raise a `ValueError` on arrays.

cards.title:
What does this print?

```python
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3))
```
cards.body:
A 2×3 array with rows `[0 1 2]` and `[3 4 5]`.

**`reshape`** gives the same elements a new shape. `np.arange(6)` is 0 to 5 in one line; reshaped to `(2, 3)`, it is filled row by row, so the first row takes 0, 1, 2 and the second takes 3, 4, 5.

Watch out: The number of elements must stay the same. `.reshape(4, 2)` on these 6 elements raises a `ValueError`.

Tip: You may write `-1` for one length and NumPy works it out: `np.arange(6).reshape(3, -1)` has shape `(3, 2)`.

cards.title: What is **row-major order** (C order), and how does an array use it in memory?
cards.body:
Memory is one long line of bytes; row-major order stores a 2-D array row by row, so the last index changes fastest.

The array `[[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]` is laid out in memory as 0 1 2 3 4 5. For a table with `C` columns, element `[i, j]` sits $i \times C + j$ items from the start. NumPy uses this layout by default, and so does the C language.

Why it matters: Walking along a row visits neighboring memory, which is fast. Walking down a column makes big jumps, which is slower.

Example: In the array above, `[1, 0]` is item $1 \times 3 + 0 = 3$, which holds the value 3.

Watch out: Some languages, such as Fortran, store column by column instead. That is column-major order.
cards.searchQuery: numpy row-major c order memory layout array
refs: NumPy User Guide: the absolute basics for beginners

cards.title: What is an array's **dtype**?
cards.body:
The dtype (data type) is the one type shared by every element of an array; it fixes how many bytes each value takes and how those bytes are read.

You read it with `a.dtype`. The digits in a dtype's name are the number of bits: `float32` is a 32-bit floating-point number, `int8` is an 8-bit integer, `uint8` is an 8-bit unsigned integer. These are the number formats from earlier, now chosen per array.

Example: `np.zeros(3).dtype` is `float64`, because NumPy makes floats 64 bits wide unless you ask otherwise. `np.zeros(3, dtype=np.float32)` asks for 32 bits instead.

Tip: Divide the bits by 8 to get bytes per element: `float32` is 4 bytes.
cards.searchQuery: numpy dtype definition float64 float32 int8 bits

cards.title: How many bytes does one **float16** element take in a NumPy array? (Number only.)
cards.body:
2

A dtype's size in bytes is its bit count divided by 8. For NumPy's fixed-size types:

- `float64`: 8 bytes
- `float32`: 4 bytes
- `float16`: 2 bytes
- `int32`: 4 bytes
- `int8` and `uint8`: 1 byte each

NumPy calls this per-element size the **itemsize**, and you read it as `a.itemsize`.

Key idea: These sizes are fixed by the type, not by the value. The number 0 in a `float64` array still takes 8 bytes.

Tip: Memorize 8, 4, 2, 1. Each step down in precision halves the memory.
cards.searchQuery: numpy float16 itemsize bytes per element dtype sizes

cards.title: How do you compute an array's memory use from its **itemsize**, and what is **nbytes**?
cards.body:
nbytes = size × itemsize: the number of elements times the bytes taken by each one.

`a.nbytes` gives this total directly. It counts the element data only, not the small bookkeeping NumPy keeps about the array.

Example: One million `float32` values take $1{,}000{,}000 \times 4 = 4{,}000{,}000$ bytes, which is 4 MB. The same million values as `float64` take 8 MB, and as `int8` only 1 MB.

Tip: Since 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes here, a million elements at 4 bytes each is an easy 4 MB to remember.
cards.searchQuery: numpy nbytes size times itemsize array memory

cards.title: What does the array method **`astype`** do?
cards.body:
`a.astype(dtype)` returns a new array with every element converted to the given dtype; the original array is left unchanged.

Example: `b = np.array([1, 2, 3]).astype(np.float32)` gives `[1. 2. 3.]` as `float32`, and the source array keeps its old dtype.

Watch out: Because the result is a new array, writing `a.astype(np.int8)` on its own line does nothing useful. Keep the result: `a = a.astype(np.int8)` or `b = a.astype(np.int8)`.

Tip: Converting to a smaller type can lose information. Converting to a larger type, such as `uint8` to `float32`, is safe.
cards.searchQuery: numpy astype convert dtype returns new array

cards.title:
What does this print?

```python
import numpy as np
a = np.array([200, 100], dtype=np.uint8)
print(a * 2)
```
cards.body:
`[144 200]`

A `uint8` holds 0 to 255. The product $200 \times 2 = 400$ does not fit, so it wraps around: $400 - 256 = 144$. The second product, $100 \times 2 = 200$, fits and stays as it is.

Watch out: There is no error and no warning. The array arithmetic silently gives the wrapped value.

Tip: To avoid wrap-around, convert first to a wider type: `a.astype(np.int32) * 2` gives `[400 200]`.
cards.searchQuery: numpy uint8 overflow wrap around 200 times 2 144

cards.title: Why is it false that a NumPy integer array can hold integers of any size, like a Python `int`?
cards.body:
False: each element has a fixed width (an `int64` spans $-2^{63}$ to $2^{63}-1$), so a result outside that range wraps around; only Python's own `int` grows without limit.

Example: `np.array([2**62]) * 4` should be $2^{64}$, but in a 64-bit integer array it comes out as `[0]`. In plain Python, `2**62 * 4` is exactly 18446744073709551616.

Why: A fixed width is what lets NumPy pack elements tightly and use the processor's own integer instructions. It is the same limit a C `int64_t` has.

Watch out: If you need huge exact integers, use plain Python ints. If you need a wide range of sizes, use floats.
cards.searchQuery: numpy integer overflow fixed width int64 vs python int

cards.title:
What does this print?

```python
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.9, -1.9])
print(a.astype(np.int32))
```
cards.body:
`[ 1 -1]`

Converting a float to an integer with `astype` drops the fractional part, which means it truncates toward zero. So 1.9 becomes 1 and -1.9 becomes -1. It does not round to 2 and -2, and it does not floor -1.9 to -2.

Tip: If you want rounding, round first and then convert: `np.round(a).astype(np.int32)` gives `[ 2 -2]`.

Watch out: The leading space in `[ 1 -1]` is only print alignment, so that the minus sign has room. The values are 1 and -1.
cards.searchQuery: numpy astype float to int truncates toward zero

cards.title: Why do machine-learning programs on small devices prefer **float32** or **int8** over **float64**?
cards.body:
Smaller types cut memory and data movement: float32 is half the size of float64, int8 is an eighth, and ML rarely needs 64-bit precision.

Memory is the first limit on a small device. A model with one million weights needs 8 MB as float64, 4 MB as float32 and 1 MB as int8. A microcontroller may have only a few hundred kilobytes of RAM.

Why it matters: Moving data costs far more energy than arithmetic. Horowitz's 45 nm figures, per 32-bit operation, are about 640 pJ for a DRAM read against 3.7 pJ for a float multiply. Fewer bytes per value means fewer reads.

Watch out: The 45 nm figures are from 2014 and are only a guide to proportions, not the numbers of today's chips.
cards.searchQuery: float32 int8 instead of float64 embedded ml memory energy
refs: Horowitz, "Computing's Energy Problem (and what we can do about it)", ISSCC 2014

cards.title: A camera frame is 224 × 224 pixels with 3 color channels (red, green, blue), one number per channel. How many bytes does it take as a NumPy `float32` array? (Number only.)
cards.body:
602,112 bytes

Count the elements first: $224 \times 224 \times 3 = 50{,}176 \times 3 = 150{,}528$ numbers.

Then use nbytes = size × itemsize. A `float32` takes 4 bytes, so $150{,}528 \times 4 = 602{,}112$ bytes, about 602 kB.

Why it matters: The same frame stored as `uint8` takes just 150,528 bytes, one quarter as much. Cameras usually deliver `uint8`, and converting to `float32` quadruples the memory.

Tip: Do the check in code with `np.zeros((224, 224, 3), dtype=np.float32).nbytes`, which gives 602112.

cards.title: What is **vectorization**, and what is an **element-wise operation**?
cards.body:
Vectorization means writing one whole-array expression, such as `a * 2 + 1`, instead of a Python loop; the element-wise operation (the same step applied to every element on its own) then runs inside NumPy.

With `a = np.array([1, 2, 3])`, the expression `a * 2 + 1` gives `[3 5 7]`. First every element is doubled, then 1 is added to every element. No `for` is written.

Why: The code is shorter, easier to read, and faster, as a later card explains.

Watch out: `*` between two arrays is element-wise multiplication, not the matrix product. Matrix products have their own operator, `@`.

cards.title: What is a **reduction** in NumPy?
cards.body:
A reduction combines the elements of an array into fewer numbers, usually one: `sum`, `mean`, `max` and `min` are the common ones.

With `a = np.array([3, 1, 4, 1])`: `a.sum()` is 9, `a.mean()` is 2.25, `a.max()` is 4 and `a.min()` is 1.

Example: The average of 1000 temperature readings is `temps.mean()`. A thousand numbers go in; one comes out.

Tip: Called with no extra arguments, a reduction uses every element. Adding an axis argument, shown on a later card, reduces along one direction only.

refs: NumPy User Guide: Universal functions (ufunc) basics

cards.title: What is a **universal function (ufunc)** in NumPy?
cards.body:
A ufunc is a function, such as `np.sqrt` or `np.add`, that applies the same operation to every element of an array in fast compiled code.

`np.sqrt(np.array([1, 4, 9]))` gives `[1. 2. 3.]`. Even the operators are ufuncs in disguise: `a + b` calls `np.add(a, b)` and does the same thing.

Why it matters: Ufuncs are the building blocks of vectorized code. If a step can be written as a ufunc, you get the loop for free.

Watch out: Python's `math.sqrt` only accepts a single number. Given an array of several elements, it raises a `TypeError`.

cards.title: Why is a vectorized NumPy expression usually much faster than the same Python loop?
cards.body:
The loop runs as compiled code over numbers packed together in memory, instead of Python carrying out one slow interpreted step, with its type checks, for each element.

In a Python loop, every pass asks the interpreter to look up the values, check their types and build a result. NumPy does that once, then runs a tight compiled loop over one block of identically typed numbers. Neighboring numbers also arrive in the processor's cache together, which speeds up reading.

Watch out: The gain shows up on large arrays. For an array of three elements the fixed cost of calling NumPy can make it no faster, or even slower.

Tip: Do not trust a hunch. Time both versions, as the `timeit` card shows.

cards.title:
This loop converts Celsius readings to Fahrenheit. Write one line that replaces the whole loop and gives the same `temps_f`.

```python
import numpy as np
temps_c = np.array([0.0, 100.0])
temps_f = np.zeros(2)
for i in range(2):
    temps_f[i] = temps_c[i] * 9 / 5 + 32
```
cards.body:
`temps_f = temps_c * 9 / 5 + 32`

Arithmetic with numbers works on a whole array at once. NumPy multiplies every element by 9, divides by 5 and adds 32, producing `[ 32. 212.]`, the same as the loop.

Key idea: Take the expression from inside the loop and replace `temps_c[i]` with the whole array `temps_c`. The `[i]` and the loop both disappear.

Watch out: This works because each result depends only on its own input element. A loop where each step needs the previous result usually cannot be rewritten this way.

cards.title:
Each row holds one moment in time and each column one sensor. What does this print?

```python
import numpy as np
readings = np.array([[20, 5],
                     [22, 7],
                     [24, 9]])
print(readings.mean(axis=0))
```
cards.body:
`[22.  7.]`

The **axis argument** names the axis that gets collapsed. With `axis=0` the rows collapse, so each column is averaged on its own: $(20+22+24)/3 = 22$ for sensor 0 and $(5+7+9)/3 = 7$ for sensor 1.

Mnemonic: The axis you name disappears from the shape. Here `(3, 2)` becomes `(2,)`: one mean per sensor.

Tip: `readings.mean(axis=1)` collapses the columns instead and gives one mean per moment in time: `[12.5 14.5 16.5]`.

cards.title:
The array holds a classifier's scores for three classes. What does this print?

```python
import numpy as np
x = np.array([0.1, 0.7, 0.2])
print(x.max(), x.argmax())
```
cards.body:
`0.7 1`

`max()` returns the largest value, 0.7. **`argmax()`** returns the position (index) of that largest value, which is 1.

Why it matters: The predicted class of a classifier is the position of its highest score, so `argmax` is how a score vector turns into an answer.

Watch out: If the largest value appears twice, `argmax` returns the first position. For `np.array([3, 9, 2, 9])` it returns 1, not 3.

cards.title:
What does `t` hold in this code?

```python
import timeit
t = timeit.timeit("sum(range(100))", number=1000)
```
cards.body:
The total time in seconds for all 1000 runs of the statement, not the time of one run.

**`timeit`** runs a statement many times and adds up the clock time, because a single run is often too short to measure reliably. To get the time per run, divide: `t / 1000`.

Example: To compare a loop with an array expression, time each with the same `number` and compare the two totals. The smaller total is the faster version.

Watch out: If you leave out `number`, it defaults to 1,000,000 runs, which can take a long time for a slow statement.

cards.title: What is **broadcasting** in NumPy?
cards.body:
Broadcasting is NumPy's way of combining arrays of different shapes element by element, by stretching the smaller one along axes where its length is 1 or missing.

The simplest case is a single number: `np.array([1, 2, 3]) + 10` gives `[11 12 13]`, as if the 10 were repeated three times. The same idea works for a table plus a row.

Example: Adding `np.array([10, 20, 30])` to a 2×3 table adds the same row to each table row.

Key idea: Broadcasting lets you write `table + row` with no loop and no hand-made copies.
cards.searchQuery: numpy broadcasting definition different shapes stretch

cards.title: State the NumPy **broadcasting rules**.
cards.body:
Compare the two shapes from the right: in each position the sizes must be equal or one of them must be 1, and a missing size counts as 1.

The right-hand end is the **trailing dimension**. A length-1 axis is a **singleton dimension**, and it is the one that gets stretched. The result's size in each position is the larger of the two.

Example: Shapes `(2, 3)` and `(3,)` work: the trailing 3 matches 3, and the missing size counts as 1. The result is `(2, 3)`. Shapes `(2, 3)` and `(2,)` fail: the trailing 3 meets 2, which are unequal and neither is 1.

Watch out: Comparing from the left is the classic mistake. Always start from the last number.
cards.searchQuery: numpy broadcasting rules compare shapes from right equal or 1

cards.title: Why does broadcasting not waste memory when a small array is combined with a huge one?
cards.body:
NumPy does not build a stretched copy of the small array: it reuses the small array's data again and again while it works through the result.

The picture of "stretching" is only a way of thinking. Adding one number to an array of a million elements does not first create a second array of a million copies of that number.

Why it matters: Broadcasting is cheap in memory as well as in typing, which matters on small devices.

Watch out: The result is still a real new array of the full size. Broadcasting saves the stretched input, not the output.
cards.searchQuery: numpy broadcasting no copies memory reuse small array

cards.title: What does **`np.newaxis`** do inside an index, and why use it?
cards.body:
It inserts a new axis of length 1 at that position, for example turning shape `(3,)` into `(3, 1)`, so a 1-D array can be made to line up as a column.

For `x = np.array([1, 2, 3])`, `x[:, np.newaxis]` has shape `(3, 1)` and `x[np.newaxis, :]` has shape `(1, 3)`. `x.reshape(3, 1)` gives the same shape as the first.

Why: A new length-1 axis is a singleton dimension, which broadcasting is able to stretch. That is how you point a 1-D array down a column instead of across a row.

Tip: `np.newaxis` is another name for `None`, so you may also see `x[:, None]`.
cards.searchQuery: numpy newaxis add axis length 1 column vector shape

cards.title: Array `a` has shape `(3, 1)` and `b` has shape `(4,)`. What is the shape of `a + b`, and what is entry `[i, j]` of the result?
cards.body:
The shape is `(3, 4)`, and entry `[i, j]` is `a[i, 0] + b[j]`.

Line the shapes up from the right: `(3, 1)` against `(4,)`, which counts as `(1, 4)`. In the last position 1 meets 4, giving 4. In the first position 3 meets 1, giving 3.

Example: With `a = [[0], [10], [20]]` and `b = [0, 1, 2, 3]`, the result has three rows: `[0 1 2 3]`, `[10 11 12 13]` and `[20 21 22 23]`. Each row adds one value of `a` to all of `b`.

Key idea: A column against a row gives a whole table with one entry for every pairing.

cards.title:
What does this print?

```python
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[1, 2],
              [3, 6],
              [5, 10]])
print(X - X.mean(axis=0))
```
cards.body:
A 3×2 array with rows `[-2. -4.]`, `[0. 0.]` and `[2. 4.]`: each column has had its own mean subtracted.

`X.mean(axis=0)` is `[3. 6.]`, with shape `(2,)`. The shapes `(3, 2)` and `(2,)` match at the trailing 2, so the row of means is stretched down all three rows and subtracted from each.

Why it matters: Centering each column on zero is a common first step before feeding data to a model. Broadcasting does it in one line.

Tip: The new column means are zero: for the first column, $-2 + 0 + 2 = 0$.
cards.searchQuery: numpy subtract column mean broadcasting center data axis=0

cards.title:
This raises a `ValueError`. Why, and how do you change one line so the result has shape `(3, 4)`?

```python
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((3, 4))
b = np.ones(3)
print(a + b)
```
cards.body:
The shapes `(3, 4)` and `(3,)` have a **shape mismatch**: from the right 4 meets 3. Fix it by making `b` a column: `b[:, np.newaxis]` (shape `(3, 1)`) or `b.reshape(3, 1)`.

NumPy's message reads "operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (3,4) (3,)". Read the shapes it prints, then check them from the right.

Example: After the fix, `a + b[:, np.newaxis]` adds `b[i]` to every element of row `i`. The shapes `(3, 4)` and `(3, 1)` give `(3, 4)`.

Watch out: A `(3,)` array is a row, not a column. It lines up with the last axis, which here has length 4.
cards.searchQuery: numpy broadcast error shapes 3,4 and 3 fix newaxis reshape

cards.title:
What does this print?

```python
import numpy as np
s = np.array([[1, 2, 3],
              [10, 20, 30]])
print(s - s.max(axis=1)[:, np.newaxis])
```
cards.body:
A 2×3 array with rows `[-2 -1 0]` and `[-20 -10 0]`: each row has had its own largest value subtracted.

`s.max(axis=1)` gives one maximum per row, `[3 30]`, with shape `(2,)`. Subtracting it directly would line `(2,)` up with the trailing axis of length 3 and fail. Adding `[:, np.newaxis]` makes it `(2, 1)`, a column that stretches across each row.

Why it matters: Subtracting each row's maximum is a common trick in machine-learning code to keep numbers small before further steps.

Key idea: Reducing along `axis=1` gives per-row results. To combine them with the original, turn them back into a column.
cards.searchQuery: numpy subtract row maximum axis=1 newaxis broadcasting

cards.title: What is the difference between a **view** and a **copy** of a NumPy array?
cards.body:
A view is a new array object that shares the original's data in memory; a copy has its own separate data.

Changing an element through a view changes the original too, because there is only one set of numbers. Changing a copy never touches the original.

Example: With `a = np.arange(5)`, the slice `v = a[1:3]` is a view of the middle of `a`. The call `c = a.copy()` makes a full independent copy.

Why: A view costs almost no memory and no time, since nothing is duplicated. That is why NumPy uses views when it can.

Tip: When you need independent data, say so explicitly with `.copy()`.

cards.title: What is the **dot product** of two 1-D arrays of the same length?
cards.body:
Multiply the matching elements and add up the products: $a \cdot b = \sum_i a_i b_i$.

Example: For `a = [1, 2, 3]` and `b = [4, 5, 6]`: $1 \cdot 4 + 2 \cdot 5 + 3 \cdot 6 = 4 + 10 + 18 = 32$. In NumPy, `a @ b` or `np.dot(a, b)` gives 32.

Why it matters: A dot product of length $K$ takes $K$ multiply-accumulates (MACs), which is $2K$ FLOPs. A neural-network neuron computes exactly this: inputs times weights, summed.

Watch out: The lengths must match. Arrays of length 3 and 2 raise a `ValueError`.

cards.title: What shape rule must hold for **matrix multiplication** `A @ B`, and what shape does the result have?
cards.body:
The inner dimensions must match: an $M \times K$ matrix times a $K \times N$ matrix gives an $M \times N$ matrix, at a cost of $M \cdot N \cdot K$ MACs.

Each entry of the result is the dot product of one row of `A` with one column of `B`. That dot product has $K$ terms, and there are $M \cdot N$ entries.

Example: Shapes `(2, 3) @ (3, 4)` give `(2, 4)`, using $2 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 = 24$ MACs. Shapes `(2, 3) @ (2, 3)` fail: the inner sizes 3 and 2 differ.

Tip: Write the shapes side by side, `(M, K) (K, N)`, and the two middle numbers must be equal. They vanish, leaving `(M, N)`.
cards.searchQuery: matrix multiplication shape rule inner dimensions M K N macs

cards.title: Why is it false that slicing a NumPy array gives an independent copy, as it does for a Python list?
cards.body:
False: a basic slice of an array is a view, so assigning into it changes the original; a list slice is a copy, but an array slice is not.

Example: After `v = np.arange(5)` and `w = v[1:3]`, the assignment `w[0] = 99` makes `v` equal to `[0 99 2 3 4]`. Picking elements with a list of positions, `v[[1, 2]]`, or with a Boolean mask, does make a copy.

Why: NumPy avoids copying large data when it can. A slice just points at the same memory with a different start and length.

Watch out: To keep the original safe, write `w = v[1:3].copy()`.
cards.searchQuery: numpy slice is a view not a copy modifies original

cards.title:
An **in-place operation** changes an array's existing memory instead of creating a new array. What does this print?

```python
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3)
b = a
a += 10
print(b)
```
cards.body:
`[10 11 12]`

`b = a` does not copy anything: both names refer to the same array. `a += 10` changes that array in place, so `b` sees the change. Writing `a = a + 10` instead would build a new array and point `a` at it, leaving `b` as `[0 1 2]`.

Why it matters: In place means no second array is allocated. For big arrays on a small device, that saves memory.

Watch out: This is the same aliasing you know from lists. Another name for an array is not a copy of it.
cards.searchQuery: numpy in-place += alias same array memory saving
refs: NumPy User Guide: Copies and views

cards.title:
The **transpose** `A.T` swaps rows and columns, so shape `(2, 3)` becomes `(3, 2)`. What does this print?

```python
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, 2, 3],
              [4, 5, 6]])
print(A @ A.T)
```
cards.body:
A 2×2 array with rows `[14 32]` and `[32 77]`.

The shapes are `(2, 3) @ (3, 2)`: the inner 3s match, so the result is `(2, 2)`. Each entry is a dot product of two rows of `A`: $1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot 3 = 14$, then $1 \cdot 4 + 2 \cdot 5 + 3 \cdot 6 = 32$, then $4 \cdot 4 + 5 \cdot 5 + 6 \cdot 6 = 77$.

Key idea: `A.T` is a view, so no data is copied. Only the way NumPy reads the rows and columns changes.

Watch out: `A @ A` fails here, because `(2, 3) @ (2, 3)` has unequal inner sizes.
cards.searchQuery: numpy matrix multiply A @ A.T transpose result shape

cards.title: In **Matplotlib**, what are the **figure** and the **axes**?
cards.body:
The figure is the whole canvas, the window or image file; an axes is one plot area on it, with its own x-axis, y-axis and data.

**Matplotlib** is a library for drawing graphs, and **pyplot** is its module of quick plotting functions, imported as `import matplotlib.pyplot as plt`. The call `fig, ax = plt.subplots()` makes one figure holding one axes, and you draw on the axes: `ax.plot(...)`.

Example: A figure can hold two axes side by side, for example one for voltage and one for current.

Watch out: Here "axes" is not the plural of "axis". One axes is a whole plot, and it contains an x-axis and a y-axis.

cards.title:
This draws a **line plot** (points joined by a line). Which one `ax` method call is missing so that the label `"sensor"` shows up on the figure?

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
t = np.linspace(0, 1, 100)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(t, np.sin(2 * np.pi * 5 * t), label="sensor")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Voltage (V)")
ax.set_title("Sensor signal")
```
cards.body:
`ax.legend()`

The `label="sensor"` only attaches a name to the line. Nothing displays it until you call `ax.legend()`, which draws a small key listing each labeled line.

Key idea: A good signal plot has axis labels with units (`Time (s)`, `Voltage (V)`), a title, and a legend when more than one line is drawn.

Tip: Put the unit in parentheses on every axis label. A reader should never have to guess whether the time axis is in seconds or milliseconds.

cards.title:
A **scatter plot** draws one dot per measurement, with no line between them. Which method fills the blank?

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
temp = [20, 25, 30, 35]
volts = [1.02, 1.11, 1.19, 1.31]
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.____(temp, volts)
```
cards.body:
`scatter`, so the line is `ax.scatter(temp, volts)`.

Each pair, such as (20, 1.02), becomes one dot. A scatter plot shows how two measured quantities relate, here voltage against temperature, without suggesting that the points in between exist.

Tip: `ax.plot(temp, volts, "o")` also draws dots only, using the marker `"o"` and no line.

Watch out: A line plot joins the points in the order given, so it is right for a signal over time. For unordered pairs of measurements, joining them would draw a misleading zigzag.

cards.title:
A **histogram** splits the range of the data into **bins** and draws one bar per bin. What does the height of each bar show in this code?

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
readings = [3.1, 3.3, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 3.3, 3.2]
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(readings, bins=3)
```
cards.body:
How many readings fall inside that bar's bin (its range of values).

With `bins=3`, the range from 3.1 to 3.4 is cut into three equal slices and each of the 7 readings is counted into the slice it belongs to. The three bar heights add up to 7.

Why it matters: A histogram shows the spread of repeated measurements, such as sensor noise: where most values cluster and how far they stray.

Tip: Too few bins hide the shape; too many make it ragged. Try a few values of `bins`.
cards.searchQuery: matplotlib histogram bins bar height counts measurement data

cards.title:
Frequencies run from 1 Hz to 10,000 Hz. Which call makes the x axis a **log-scale axis**?

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
f = [1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000]
gain = [1.0, 0.99, 0.7, 0.1, 0.01]
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(f, gain)
```
cards.body:
`ax.set_xscale("log")`

On a log-scale axis, equal distances mean equal ratios, so 1, 10, 100, 1000 and 10000 are spaced evenly. On a normal axis, the first three points would be squashed against the left edge.

Tip: `ax.set_yscale("log")` does the same for the y axis. Using both gives a log-log plot.

Watch out: A log axis cannot show zero or negative values, because no power of 10 equals them.

cards.title:
What does this code do?

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 4])
fig.savefig("curve.png", dpi=150)
```
cards.body:
It writes the figure to a PNG file called `curve.png` in the current folder.

The file type comes from the extension in the name. The `dpi` setting (dots per inch) controls resolution: a higher value gives a larger, sharper image.

Watch out: In a script, call `savefig` before `plt.show()`. Once the window is closed, the figure can be gone and you may save an empty image.

Tip: Save as PNG for images with sharp lines and text, and keep `dpi=150` or more when the picture is going into a report.
